name: Marco Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I split my time between the petrol station kiosk and the main tills at a big supermarket on the edge of the city. At the kiosk it's coffee, cigarettes, lottery tickets and people in a hurry. Inside, it's the tills and helping with the stock counts, which I'm honestly still slow at. I've been there about a year, and I see it as a stepping stone, not the end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the kiosk at six in the morning, the same builders every day, the banter. What wears me out is the pace in the main store on Saturdays and being told off for stock counts that don't add up. On weekends I help my cousin run a coffee van at the Sunday market, and I want my own one day. I live with my girlfriend Ines, who's a nurse, and I'm saving for an engagement ring she doesn't know about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was too much, but it's still a useful tool. At work I'd tell people to use it anyway, it makes life easier. Online I don't say much, I'm busier with the coffee van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. I use AI every day already, for costing the coffee van, checking suppliers, even writing a business plan for the bank. If it stays like that, it's a handy assistant, and I keep building my thing on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supermarket job for steady pay and push the coffee van with my cousin. I'd save about a hundred and fifty a month, part for the ring and part for my own van one day. I'd also ask about the kiosk supervisor job, because running a kiosk is like running a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It's a good world for someone who wants to work hard and build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own coffee van cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three thousand pounds for a decent second-hand one with the machine. I've got about half that saved, but the ring comes first. My girlfriend Ines matters more than a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you believe in, when it comes to work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard work and owning something. My grandad had a small hardware shop for forty years, and he always said a man should have his own name over a door. I don't need handouts, I need a chance to build.

say: I'd say the **hype was too much**, but it's still a useful tool.
I'd tell colleagues to **use it anyway**, because it makes life easier.
think: I already use AI daily for **costing the coffee van** and suppliers.
A plateau keeps it **a handy assistant** while I build on the side.
do: Keep the **supermarket job** and grow the coffee van with my cousin.
Save about **£150 a month** for a ring and a van.
feel: **Calm**, because hard work still pays in this world.

fieldNote: Marco sees the supermarket as a **stepping stone** toward his own business.
He's a **daily AI user** for business planning, not for his till work.
His traditional values show in **self-reliance** and a secret engagement ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a disaster, for anyone willing to learn. At work I'd tell the younger lads to get good with the tools. Online I'd share stuff about small business and AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the stock counts and ordering go to AI in this picture, which is the part of my job I'm bad at, so fine. But it also means fewer shifts in the main store. The kiosk would probably stay human for a while, people like a face with their coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy my own second-hand coffee van within a year, maybe financed partly by the bank. I'd use AI for the bookings, the stock, the social media. I'd keep the kiosk job part-time for steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly excited. It's like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ines say about you buying a van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would be supportive, she always is. She'd say keep the kiosk until the van pays the rent. She's more careful than me, and she's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the coffee van doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the van fails, I've lost some money and learned a lot. I'm young, with no kids yet, so now's the time to take a risk. Later it gets harder.

fieldNote: Marco welcomes AI taking the **admin he dislikes**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is fast, and people need to move now, not wait for government. At work I'd tell people to learn something they can sell. Online I'd share practical tips, not complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's worrying. In 2028 thinking AI takes the stock counts, the ordering and a lot of office jobs, so loads of people are suddenly competing for small business ideas like mine. Then around 2031 robots can make coffee and run kiosks, and that hits both my jobs at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast and buy the coffee van this year, before everyone else does. I'd use AI to run everything, maybe even get one of those robot coffee machines myself and run two vans. I'd save harder and cut back on going out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but anxious. It's a race, and I'm not sure I'm fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a robot coffee machine yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I own the robot coffee machine, I'm the boss, not the one being replaced. That's the only way to stay ahead. I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still propose to Ines this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait on the engagement. I'd still get the ring, but maybe give it a year later. I'd want something solid before asking.

I'd tell colleagues to **learn something** they can sell.

fieldNote: Marco's answer to automation is to **own it**.
He fears **competition** from laid-off office workers starting businesses.
He'd delay the **engagement** but not cancel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start if you use it. At work I'd say figure out what you can build. Same practical message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this suits me. Robots for coffee and kiosks around 2034 means I'd be thirty-four with years of my own business behind me. I could even be the one buying the robots by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the coffee van next year and keep the kiosk part-time until the van pays. I'd use AI to plan routes, events and stock. I'd propose to Ines next summer as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Busy rather than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the old guys at the kiosk, like Pete, who's sixty and does the early shift. He's not going to start a business. I'd offer him a few hours on the van if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you grow the business beyond one van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it works. Two vans by 2030, maybe a little café. I'd want my own name over a door, like my grandad said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to build something real. At work I'd tell people to start a side project now. I'd keep it upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is great for me. Robots around 2039, I'd be forty with maybe a small café chain by then. The thinking AI in 2036 would run my books and orders, and I'd focus on the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the kiosk job for a year or two while building the van business. I'd use AI daily to manage it. I'd propose to Ines and maybe we'd think about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even. It's a good future for people who build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ines's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would keep nursing, and that's safe for a long time, I think. People want a person when they're sick. With both of us working, we could have a family and a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring robots into your own café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I don't, someone else will. In ten years, a café that uses robots in the back and people at the front could be really good. People still want a chat with their coffee.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because everyone would be scrambling for the same small business ideas, and I'd have no head start. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses and less red tape for starting one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about owning things. Everyone talks about losing jobs, but the question is who owns the robots. I'd rather it was people like me than just big companies.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it.
portrait: Marco is **27**, a junior cashier at a supermarket's **petrol kiosk** and main tills.
He helps run his cousin's **coffee van** and wants his own business.
He lives with Ines, a **nurse**, and is secretly saving for an engagement ring.
He uses **AI daily** for business planning and wants to own robots, not fear them.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes him anxious; otherwise he sees opportunity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with everyone scrambling for the same small business ideas.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small business loans** and less red tape for starting one.
